sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Image analogy transfers a demonstrated transformation from a before/after pair (A, A') to a new query image B. Existing methods assume all changes in (A, A') should be fully transferred, limiting flexibility when users want only a subset of the demonstrated edits. We introduce Selective Image Analogy (SIA), a new setting where a single demonstration pair encodes multiple edits, and the user selects at inference time which edits to apply to B. To support this, we curate a multi-edit analogy dataset with full-edit and partial-edit targets. We then train a model that first learns to transfer the complete demonstrated transformation, and then gains selective control through a mask-aligned suppression mechanism: a token-gated LoRA that restricts adapter updates to suppressed edit tokens during denoising, paired with a concept suppression vector that weakens the selected tokens in the text embeddings before denoising. Together, these components allow SIA to suppress unwanted edits that remain visible in A', while preserving the user-selected ones, all without requiring a new demonstration pair for each edit combination. We perform extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations along with user studies to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Image editing plays crucial role across wide range of applications, including photography, film production, advertising, medical imaging, and content creation, where precise control over visual details is essential. In recent years, text-based image editing has emerged as powerful and intuitive approach, enabling users to modify images through natural language instructions [Couairon et al. 2023; 2 Amirhossein Alimohammadi, Kian Izadpanah, Bardiya Kariminia, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, and Ali Mahdavi-Amiri Zhang et al. 2023a]. While effective, relying solely on text is often insufficient, as language may struggle to capture fine-grained visual nuances, spatial relationships, or stylistic intent [Li et al. 2023; Mou et al. 2024]. As result, complementary techniques have been developed to bridge this gap, such as image composition methods that combine multiple visual elements [Song et al. 2023; Yang et al. 2023], sketch-based editing that provides explicit structural guidance [Mikaeili et al. 2023], and frameworks like ControlNet [Zhang et al. 2023b] that incorporate additional conditioning signals. Together, these approaches enhance controllability and enable more accurate and expressive image editing workflows. An alternative and powerful editing approach is image analogy, which enables the transfer of transformations from one example to another in structured way [Chen et al. 2025; Hertzmann et al. 2001; Šubrtová et al. 2023]. In this setting, pair of images 𝐴 and 𝐴 represents specific edit or transformationsuch as change in style, texture, or geometry. The goal is then to apply the same transformation to new input image 𝐵, producing corresponding output 𝐵 that reflects the edits observed between 𝐴 and 𝐴. In other words, the system learns the mapping from 𝐴 to 𝐴 and generalizes it to 𝐵, allowing consistent and controllable edits without requiring explicit textual or manual specification. This makes image analogy particularly useful for tasks where visual changes are easier to demonstrate than to describe. text prompt or reference image specifies the category of an edit, while before/after pair captures its exact visual formincluding style, shape, size, placement, magnitude, and subject-specific interactions. These relative properties are difficult to convey through text or single reference image. For example, in Fig. 1, text can specify adding an SIA logo but not its exact font; the demonstration pair directly provides this visual detail, enabling its transfer to the query subject. However, prior image analogy methods typically assume that all changes observed between 𝐴 and 𝐴 should be fully transferred to the target image 𝐵. This all-or-nothing behavior limits their flexibility in practical scenarios, where users may only want to apply subset of the edits. For example, one might wish to transfer attributes such as smile or the presence of sunglasses from 𝐴 while preserving the original pose, lighting, or background of 𝐵. By entangling multiple transformations into single mapping, these approaches make it difficult to selectively control which aspects are propagated, thereby restricting their applicability in more nuanced and user-driven editing tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce new problem setting termed Selective Image Analogy, where the transformation from 𝐴 to 𝐴 may involve multiple edits, but only subset of these edits is transferred to target image 𝐵 (see Fig. 1). Crucially, the selection of which edits to apply is guided by text, allowing users to specify their intent at high level while still leveraging the rich visual cues embedded in the example pair. This formulation combines the strengths of text-based editingflexibility and semantic controlwith the expressiveness of image analogy, enabling more precise and user-driven manipulation of visual content. To solve this problem, we design SIA so that the same demonstration pair (𝐴, 𝐴) can support different user-selected outputs. The model first learns the standard analogy behavior, transferring the full transformation shown between 𝐴 and 𝐴 to new query image 𝐵. We then make this behavior selective through an edit-token suppression mask, which marks the edits the user does not want to transfer. This mask controls suppression at two aligned points: during denoising, it applies token-gated LoRA only to the suppressed edit tokens; before denoising, it weakens the corresponding text embeddings along edit directions estimated from positive and negative prompt pairs. This allows SIA to suppress unwanted edits that remain visible in 𝐴, while preserving the edits selected by the user without requiring new demonstration pair for each edit combination. We demonstrate the efficacy and generalizability of our method through extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations, as well as series of ablation studies that justify our design choices, all while maintaining lightweight and training-efficient framework that requires no per-query optimization or new demonstration pairs. Therefore, our contributions are as follows: We introduce Selective Image Analogy, new image analogy setting that, to our knowledge, is the first to allow multiedit before/after demonstration to be selectively transferred to new image. We introduce mask-aligned suppression mechanism that localizes suppression to user-selected edit phrases, enabling unwanted edits to be blocked even when they remain visible in the demonstration. We also curate multi-edit training examples with full-edit and partial-edit targets, allowing the model to learn both complete and selective transfer.

sections.title:
2 Related Works
2.1
sections.content: Image editing. Diffusion-based image editing was popularized by SDEdit [Meng et al. 2022], which edits an input image by adding noise and denoising it under target condition. Later, instruction-based editors made this process more accessible by allowing users to describe edits with natural-language commands [Brack et al. 2024; Brooks et al. 2023; Kawar et al. 2023; Mokady et al. 2023]. Since text alone is often not enough for precise control, recent works incorporate additional signals such as structural guidance with ControlNet [Zhang et al. 2023b], reference-based conditioning [Ye et al. 2023], and attention-sharing mechanisms [Alimohammadi et al. 2025; Cao et al. 2023; Mikaeili et al. 2026; Xu et al. 2024]. More recently, transformer-based diffusion and flow models have shown strong versatility across local and global editing tasks [Labs et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025]. Our work builds on this progress, but moves toward selective visual analogies, where the edit is given by before/after demonstration and only the user-selected parts of that demonstration are transferred. 2.2 Image analogy. In image analogy, the user demonstrates an edit with before/after example, and the edit is transferred to another image, which shares similarity with the example pair. Classical Image Analogies [Hertzmann et al. 2001] introduced the general formulation of transferring the edit through example-based local visual matching. Deep Image Analogy [Liao et al. 2017] extended this idea to semantically related image pairs by matching deep features, enabling visual attribute transfer across large appearance gaps, while Structural Analogy [Benaim et al. 2021] learns generative mapping between the structures of two images from single pair. With the advent of stronger generative models such as diffusion models, image analogy was revisited using noise inversion techniques guided by the CLIP embedding space [Šubrtová et al. 2023]. Alternative approaches leveraged visual prompting and in-context learning, where example pairs are placed together with the query image as visual context [Bar et al. 2022; Gu et al. 2024; Sun et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2023]. The intuition is that, when these images are given jointly to diffusion transformer, the model can compare them through attention and infer the transformation to apply, without optimizing separate model for each test example. Building on this direction, Edit Transfer [Chen et al. 2025] learns visual relations from source-target editing examples and applies them to new query images. LoRWeB [Manor et al. 2026] improves generalization by dynamically composing basis of LoRA modules for different analogy types. VIRAL [Li et al. 2026] further studies visual in-context reasoning with diffusion transformers using roleaware multi-image conditioning and expert mixing. These methods show that visual demonstrations can capture transformations that are difficult to express with language alone, including spatial, nonrigid, and compositional edits. However, they generally transfer the demonstrated transformation as whole. In contrast, our setting considers demonstrations where 𝐴 𝐴 contains multiple edits, and the user may want to transfer only selected subset while keeping the same demonstration fixed.

sections.title: 2.3 Controllable image editing.
sections.content: Our work broadly falls within the domain of controllable image editing, where users are given more direct control over which visual changes are applied and how strongly they appear. Concept Sliders [Gandikota et al. 2024] learns LoRA sliders for visual concepts, allowing continuous control over semantics. TARA [Peng et al. 2026] uses token masks to reduce interference between LoRA modules in multi-concept personalization. SliderEdit [Zarei et al. 2025] similarly restricts LoRA updates to selected instruction tokens, enabling fine-grained control over different parts of multi-instruction edit. Another line of work controls generation and editing through meaningful directions in learned representation spaces. Early methods study such directions in GAN latent spaces [Shen et al. 2020] or use CLIP guidance to manipulate StyleGAN representations [Patashnik et al. 2021]. More recent diffusion and flow-based methods apply similar ideas to text embeddings and intermediate activations. Continuous Subject-Specific Attribute Control [Baumann et al. 2025] estimates CLIP directions from contrastive prompts. SHIFT [Konovalova et al. 2026] builds steering vectors from paired positive and neutral prompts and applies them to intermediate activations in DiT-based flow models, while Diffusion Sliders [Ekin and Gandelsman 2026] derives text-encoder directions from contrastive prompt pairs for controllable steering. These works control visual changes through token-level mechanisms, adapters, and representation-space directions, and our proposed method shares this spirit. However, applying these techniques SIA: Selective Image Analogy 3 to selective image analogy is non-trivial: the edit to suppress is not absent from the inputit remains fully visible in 𝐴so the model cannot simply ignore it. Text removal alone is insufficient, since the visual demonstration actively reintroduces the suppressed edit signal. This helps suppression operate at two aligned stages: weakening the text-conditioning signal before denoising and gating the adapter updates during denoising, both localized to the specific edit tokens. Our work is therefore the first to make single visual analogy demonstration selectable, allowing subset of edits to be transferred from the same fixed before/after pair.

a visual before/after demonstration. Given a source image 𝐴, its
edited version 𝐴′, and a target image 𝐵, our goal is to transfer only

Given demonstration pair (𝐴, 𝐴 ) containing multiple edits and query image 𝐵, the model transfers only the user-selected edits to produce 𝐵. In this example, green textual tokens indicate retained edits that should be applied to 𝐵, while red textual tokens indicate suppressed edits that should not be transferred, even though they are present in 𝐴. The visual analogy guides the overall edit transfer, while the colored textual tokens specify which edits are retained or suppressed using selective token suppression and the Concept Suppression Vector (CSV). Unlike standard image analogy [Hertzmann et al. 2001], which transfers the full demonstrated transformation, SIA keeps the same before/after pair fixed while allowing selective control over which edits are applied. This setting differs from ordinary text-guided editing because the model also receives the visual pair (𝐴, 𝐴) as conditioning: since 𝐴 already contains all demonstrated edits, simply removing an edit from the prompt is insufficientthe model can still infer and transfer it from 𝐴. Rather than constructing separate demonstration pair for each possible subset (which would be impractical), we use one full demonstration pair and control which edits are transferred at inference time via token-level suppression mask that marks phrases corresponding to suppressed edits; SIA first learns to transfer all demonstrated edits and then applies this mask to selectively block them, as described below.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate SIA on multiple demonstrated edits using our MultiEdit Analogy Dataset. Our goal is to evaluate selective transfer quality, the contribution of ExLoRA and CSV over prompt-based suppression, and robustness across edit types and multi-edit settings. Two user studies evaluating the same criterion are reported in Sec. B.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup.
sections.content: We evaluate SIA on Flux.2-Klein [Black Forest Labs 2025] in concatmode, with 𝐴, 𝐴, and 𝐵 as conditions. Both AnaLoRA and ExLoRA use rank 𝑟 =16, learning rate 5105, and up to 50K steps, with batch sizes of 16 and 24 respectively. At inference, we use 28 denoising steps with ExLoRA scale 1.0. Each CSV direction is estimated from 64 prompt pairs per edit, cached once, and applied with suppression strength 𝜆𝑖 (Eq. 7) selected from {0, 75, 150, 225, 300}. We compare with VisualCloze [Li et al. 2025], RelationAdapter [Gong et al. 2025], LoRWeB [Manor et al. 2026], and Edit Transfer [Chen et al. 2025].

sections.content: Fig. 5 shows results of SIA across set of selective image analogy tasks. The examples cover local object additions, facial expression changes, background replacements, and style transfer. In contrast, SIA better separates the demonstrated edits: it preserves the retained transformations, suppresses the user-selected edit, and maintains the identity and overall structure of the query image 𝐵. sections.title: 5.4 Ablation Study.
sections.content: We ablate the two selective suppression components of SIA in Tab. 2 and the supplementary material (Sec. F). In addition to Retained Accuracy and Preservation, we report VLM-based Suppression score (Supp.), measuring whether suppressed edits are absent from the output. AnaLoRA remains active in all variants as the base visualanalogy capability. Without ExLoRA and CSV, the model transfers nearly the full transformation from 𝐴. CSV alone weakens the suppressed edits text signal but lacks learned suppression pathway, while ExLoRA alone provides token-local suppression but leaves residual semantic evidence in the prompt embeddings. Combining both yields the strongest suppression and overall performance. The slight drop in Retained Accuracy reflects the trade-off between suppression strength and retained-edit fidelity, while visual ablations confirm their complementary roles.

sections.title: 6 Limitations, Future Work and Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Selective Image Analogy, novel problem setting that, to our knowledge, is the first to enable selective transfer from multi-edit visual demonstration. Unlike prior image analogy methods that treat the demonstrated transformation as an indivisible whole, SIA allows user to choose which edits from single before/after pair are applied to new query image, while suppressing the resteven when the suppressed edits remain visible in the demonstration. To support this setting, we constructed multi-edit analogy dataset and proposed mask-aligned suppression mechanism combining AnaLoRA for full-transfer learning, ExLoRA for Fig. 3. Advantage of demonstration-based specification. Text conveys the category of an edit but not its exact form. In each row, the demonstration specifies the exact visual form of the edit, including its structure, shape, and color, which text-based editing fails to reproduce, while SIA matches the demonstrated transformation. prompt. This gives each baseline access to the user-desired edit subset, while keeping the visual demonstration fixed. The comparison, therefore, tests whether each method can avoid copying suppressed edits from 𝐴, where the full transformation remains visually present. Fig. 4 shows qualitative comparisons with baselines.

sections.title: 5.3 Quantitative Evaluation.
sections.content: We report both CLIP-based and VLM-based metrics. For CLIP-based evaluation, we report two directional metrics. CLIP-Dir Image is the image-image directional metric that measures agreement with the demonstrated image-space transformation. CLIP-Dir Retained measures whether the generated output moves in the direction of the retained edit descriptions, making it suitable for selective transfer. For semantic evaluation, we use VLM-based protocol, following the recent use of vision-language models for assessing image editing quality and human-aligned preferences [Huang et al. 2025]. Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct [Bai et al. 2025] and Gemma 4 [Gemma Team et al. 2026] are used as independent judges; results with Gemma 3 [Gemma Team et al. 2025] as third judge are reported in the supplementary material. Each VLM is given the demonstration pair (𝐴, 𝐴), the query image 𝐵, the generated output ˆ𝐵, and the lists of retained and suppressed edits. We report three VLM metrics. Retained Accuracy measures the quality of applying the retained edits. Preservation measures whether the output maintains the identity, layout, and unrelated content of 𝐵. Edit Recall measures the fraction of retained edits detected in the output. Tab. 1 compares SIA against recent visual analogy baselines. SIA achieves the highest retained-edit accuracy and edit recall under both VLM judges (and under Gemma 3; see the supplementary material), and also obtains the best CLIP directional scores. Under Gemma 4, SIA also attains the highest preservation among the analogy baselines. We note that methods such as Edit Transfer 8 Amirhossein Alimohammadi, Kian Izadpanah, Bardiya Kariminia, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, and Ali Mahdavi-Amiri token-gated suppression during denoising, and CSV for weakening residual edit signals in the text embeddings before denoising. Extensive quantitative evaluations, qualitative comparisons, and user study confirm that SIA consistently outperforms existing visual analogy baselines on the selective transfer objective, demonstrating that single demonstration pair can serve as flexible, user-controllable source of edits rather than fixed, all-or-nothing transformation. While SIA currently supports up to handful of demonstrated edits, it may struggle when 𝐴 and 𝐴 differ substantially. The dataset also covers limited range of edit types and scenes, leaving out fine-grained operations such as artifact removal and complex layouts. Scaling to larger number of edits and broader edit diversity remains an interesting direction for future work. Another promising direction is compositional demonstration, where edits are drawn from multiple different before/after pairs and combined into single selective transfer, allowing users to mix demonstrated edits across sources with controllable intensity rather than being constrained to single (𝐴, 𝐴).

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: Backbone. For all experiments, we use the 9B-parameter variant of Flux.2-Klein [Black Forest Labs 2025] as the diffusion backbone. The text stream is encoded by the Qwen3 text encoder packaged with Flux.2-Klein. The diffusion pipeline concatenates the hidden states from three Qwen3 layers ({9, 18, 27}) along the channel dimension to form the per-token prompt embedding consumed by the MM-DiT blocks. As described in the main paper, ExLoRA is injected into the text-stream projections of the MM-DiT blocks. Adapters. AnaLoRA and ExLoRA are independent LoRA adapters with rank 𝑟 =16 and dropout 0. We first train AnaLoRA with batch size 16, learning rate 5105, and up to 50K optimization steps on mixture of full-transfer tuples from the two-, three-, and fouredit groups. We then merge the resulting checkpoint into the frozen backbone and train ExLoRA on top, using batch size 24 and the same learning rate. sections.title: B User Study
sections.content: Standard image-level metrics, such as LPIPS and CLIP similarity, do not fully capture the main requirement of selective image analogy, where the output must apply the retained edits, avoid the suppressed edit, and still preserve the query image 𝐵. We therefore conduct user study focused on this task-specific criterion. In each trial, participants are shown the demonstration pair (𝐴, 𝐴), the query image 𝐵, the retained edits, the edit selected for suppression, and outputs from SIA and the baseline methods in random order. Participants are asked to rank the top three outputs according to how well they satisfy the selective analogy objective, considering three factors jointly: applying the retained edits, avoiding the suppressed edit, and preserving the identity and structure of 𝐵. We collect responses from 37 participants over 15 examples and compare SIA against the baselines. For scoring, the first-ranked result receives 3 points, the second receives 2 points, the third receives 1 point, and unranked results receive 0 points. The results in Tab. 3 show that our method receives the highest average ranking score, confirming that SIA better matches the intended selective edit behavior. We additionally conduct second user study that directly compares SIA against the Text Only and Full Transfer + Removal baselines, the strongest text-conditioned alternatives to demonstration-based transfer. In each trial, participants see the demonstration pair (𝐴, 𝐴), the query image 𝐵, the retained-edit and suppressed-edit lists, and the outputs of the three methods in random order. Participants rate the Fidelity on 010 scale. Fidelity measures whether the retained edits match the demonstrated form in 𝐴 with the same style, shape, and color, and not merely the same category of edit, where low score means the retained edits are missing or bear no resemblance to 𝐴, mid-range score means the correct type of edit but different instance (for example, sunglasses of different style), and the maximum means every retained edit is present and matches the exact appearance in 𝐴. After rating all three outputs, participants additionally select the single best overall result for that sample. We collect responses from 20 participants over 8 examples. As shown in Tab. 4, SIA attains the highest Fidelity score and is chosen as the best overall result in 65.4% of trials, compared with 30.1% for Text Only and 4.4% for Full Transfer + Removal. While text-based editing often produces the correct semantic edit, it fails to reproduce the demonstrated visual form, which is precisely what the Fidelity metric penalises. Comparison to text-based editing and commercial models natural question is whether we even need the demonstration pair at all, given how strong textand reference-conditioned editors have become. To check this, we compare SIA against three additional baselines on the same test set. (i) Text Only simply runs FLUX.2-Klein-9B with the retained-edit instruction as text, with no demonstration pair involved. (ii) Full Transfer + Removal first copies over every demonstrated edit, then tries to undo the suppressed ones with text instruction. (iii) Nano Banana is commercial black-box editor that takes the full triplet (𝐴, 𝐴, 𝐵) along with the retainededit instruction; qualitative comparisons against it are shown in Sec. D. Results are reported in Tab. 5. All three baselines score high on Recall, meaning they generally produce the right kind of edit. But Recall only checks whether an edit happened. It does not check whether the edit looks like the one demonstrated in 𝐴, matching its style, shape, size, placement, and scale. That is what Retained Accuracy measures, and this is where SIA pulls ahead of every baseline  (Fig. 3)  . Full Transfer + Removal does even worse. Its removal step often changes parts of 𝐵 that should have stayed the same, which lowers its Preservation score. These metrics can still miss subtler visual mismatches, so we run second check: head-to-head comparison judged by Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct (Tab. 7). For each pair, the judge sees (𝐴, 𝐴, 𝐵), the retained-edit description, and one output from SIA next to one from either Text Only or Full Transfer + Removal. sections.title: D SIA vs Nano Banana qualitative comparison
sections.content: Beyond the analogy-based baselines evaluated in the main paper, natural question is how SIA compares against strong commercial editors that accept multiple reference images directly. We therefore compare against Nano Banana, black-box multi-reference editor, giving it the same demonstration pair (𝐴, 𝐴), the query image 𝐵, and the retained-edit instruction. Fig. 6 shows the results across range of edits, including adding sunglasses, crown, logo, beard, and lipstick. In every case, Nano Banana recognizes the correct kind of edit but does not reproduce the specific form demonstrated in 𝐴: the sunglasses and crown take on the wrong shape, the star logo is placed incorrectly, and the lipstick appears in the wrong color. SIA, by contrast, matches both the type and the appearance of each demonstrated edit while leaving the identity and structure of 𝐵 intact. This highlights key advantage of demonstration-based transfer: text or reference conditioning alone conveys what to edit, but not the precise visual form the edit should take. 14 Amirhossein Alimohammadi, Kian Izadpanah, Bardiya Kariminia, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, and Ali Mahdavi-Amiri demonstrated edits. Since no existing dataset provides this structure, we build new multi-edit analogy dataset for our task. Fig. 7 shows the generation pipeline, and Fig. 8 shows the storage layout for each sample. E.1 Edit recipes and storage format Our dataset is organized around edit recipes. An edit recipe defines the set of edits applied to all subjects in group, such as adding an object, changing the background, or changing the image style. We represent each recipe as set of edits = {𝑒1, . . . , 𝑒𝑁 }, where 𝑁 {2, 3, 4}. For each subject in recipe, we store the original image 𝐼 , the full-edit image 𝐼 , and the intermediate partial images 𝐼 for the retained edit subsets that are reachable through the sequential synthesis process. As in the main paper, denotes the retained edits and = denotes the suppressed edits. Each edit also has short natural-language description, which is used both for prompting and for constructing the contrastive pairs used by CSV (Sec. A). Training tuples are formed by pairing two subjects 𝑎 and 𝑏 from the same recipe: = 𝐼 𝐵 = 𝐼 𝑏 . 𝐴 = 𝐼 𝑎 , 𝐴 = 𝐼 𝑎 , For the query subject 𝑏, the full target 𝐵 𝑏 contains all demonR = 𝐼 strated edits, while the selective target 𝐵 𝑏 contains only the retained edits. Together, these targets provide the supervision needed for selective analogy. The full target 𝐵 teaches the model to transfer the complete demonstrated transformation, while the selective target 𝐵 teaches the model how the same demonstration should be interpreted when the mask excludes the edits in S. Concretely, every leaf directory contains the source image 𝐼 , the reference images that visually anchor each individual edit (for example, the style reference, object reference, or target expression), the sequence of composite images corresponding to partial-edit subsets, and prompt.json file that maps each composite to short natural-language instruction. Fig. 8 summarizes this layout. E.2 Two-edit data from RelationAdapter and style sources The first part of our dataset contains two-edit analogies built from subset of RelationAdapter [Gong et al. 2025]. RelationAdapter provides diverse single-edit transformations, such as changing character attributes, modifying pose, adding accessories, or altering local appearance. We treat each selected RelationAdapter pair as the first edit, and introduce second edit by applying style transformation defined by small set of predefined style reference images. We use Flux.2-Klein in style-transfer mode to synthesize both the style-only composite and the final two-edit composite. Each example therefore contains four images of the same subject: the original image, the RelationAdapter-edited image, the style-only image, and the final image that combines both edits. Since RelationAdapter provides most of the visual diversity, this subset is the main source of edit variation in our dataset. E.3 Synthetic three-edit and four-edit data The second part of our dataset contains more complex edit recipes with three or four edits. These examples are designed to expose the Fig. 6. Visual comparison with Nano Banana. Qualitative comparisons against Nano Banana, commercial multi-reference editor, show that only SIA reproduces the demonstrated edits exact visual form. Nano Banana typically identifies the correct category of edit, but fails to match the specific appearance shown in 𝐴: it renders sunglasses and the crown with the wrong shape, places the star logo in the wrong position, and produces an incorrect lipstick color. In contrast, SIA consistently matches both the type and the precise form of each demonstrated edit while preserving the identity and structure of 𝐵. Multi-Edit Analogy Dataset In multi-edit image analogy, the model must transfer demonstrated transformation from one subject to another, while also separating that transformation into its individual edit components. This requires supervision beyond standard image-editing datasets. For each subject, we need the original image, the fully edited image, and partial-edit images that correspond to different subsets of the SIA: Selective Image Analogy 15 Fig. 7. Overview of our multi-edit dataset generation pipeline. For higher-order edit settings, we start from base image and apply edits sequentially to obtain intermediate composites and the final full-edit image. For two-edit settings, we augment RelationAdapter pairs with an additional style transformation synthesized by Flux.2-Klein. All generated samples are filtered with Qwen2.5-VL to verify that the intended edits are correctly expressed. Fig. 8. Per-sample storage layout. Each leaf directory stores the source image, one reference image for each edit phrase, the sequence of composite images corresponding to retained subsets E, and prompt.json file that maps every composite to short natural-language description. model to cases where multiple edits must be suppressed at the same time while the remaining edits are preserved. For these settings, we first generate source images with Flux.2-Klein and then use the same model to synthesize the edited variants, including object additions, style changes, and background changes. Starting from the original image 𝐼 , edits are applied sequentially. We first generate the single-edit image, then the two-edit image, and finally the full multi-edit image. For three-edit recipe, this gives the progression 𝐼 𝐼 {𝑒1 } 𝐼 {𝑒1,𝑒2 } 𝐼 E, and for four-edit recipe, 𝐼 𝐼 {𝑒1 } 𝐼 {𝑒1,𝑒2 } 𝐼 {𝑒1,𝑒2,𝑒3 } 𝐼 . The three-edit group contains recipes such as one object addition with style change and background change, two object additions with style change, or two object additions with background change. The four-edit group contains single recipe that combines two object additions, one background change, and one style change. The higher-order groups are less diverse than the two-edit subset, but they serve different purpose: they teach the model to handle settings where several edits must be suppressed together. In short, Amirhossein Alimohammadi, Kian Izadpanah, Bardiya Kariminia, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, and Ali Mahdavi-Amiri the two-edit data provides most of the edit diversity, while the threeand four-edit groups encourage the same suppression behavior in more complex multi-edit cases. E.4 Vision-language filtering The sequential synthesis pipeline can introduce artifacts. An intended edit may fail to appear in composite, or an edit from an earlier step may be partially undone by later step. To remove these failure cases, we filter every leaf directory with vision-language model. For each composite 𝐼 R, we show the model the source image and the composite, then ask it to check two conditions: (i) every edit in is present, and (ii) every edit in is absent. Samples that fail either condition are discarded. We use Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct for this filtering step, with separate text-only and image-conditioned passes when needed. The text-only pass is used to paraphrase the high-level transformation label, while the image-conditioned pass is used to verify style or appearance changes. The resulting dataset therefore provides not only the full transformation between 𝐴 and 𝐴, but also the intermediate partial composites needed for selective supervision. It is also filtered so that the desired edits are present and the excluded edits are absent. E.5 Dataset Statistics and Composition Analysis This section describes how the dataset is composed and how it is split into training and test sets. In total, it contains 1,845 samples, organized into 5 categories and 238 distinct edit-recipe settings. Each category is defined by two properties: the number of edits in the recipe, 𝑁 {2, 3, 4}, and whether the subject is stylized creature (the default, majority case) or non-creature object such as vehicle or prop. Across these categories, the dataset spans five fundamental edit types: object addition, background change, style transfer, pose change, and facial expression change. Tab. 8 reports the full composition. Train/test partitioning. Overall, 1,606 samples (87.05%) are used for training and 239 (12.95%) for testing, ratio of roughly 6.72:1. This split is not applied uniformly across categories. Instead, the ratio in each category reflects the role that category plays in the dataset. The 2edits creature category is by far the largest and most varied part of the dataset, with 1,478 samples across 210 settings. It supplies most of the visual and recipe diversity, so we use almost all of it for training (98.71%) and hold out only 19 samples for testing. Every other category is majority-test: 63.16% for 2edits non-creature, 58.67% for 3edits, 61.02% for 3edits non-creature, and 57.14% for 4edits. The reasoning is simple. The large two-edit creature pool provides the training signal, while the smaller and more narrowly built categories are reserved mainly for evaluation. They let us test whether the models selective-suppression behavior carries over to more complex recipes and to different type of subject, rather than adding much training signal of their own. The settings counts follow the same pattern. The 2edits category alone accounts for 210 of the 238 settings (88.3%), yet contributes only 19 test samples. The remaining four categories together contribute just 28 settings (11.7%), but send most of their samples to the test split. Distribution across edit complexity. It is also useful to group samples purely by edit count, ignoring the creature and non-creature distinction. The subtotal rows of Tab. 8 give this view. Two-edit recipes dominate at 83.20% of all samples. This matches our design: the RelationAdapter-derived two-edit subset (Sec. E.2) supplies most of the visual and semantic diversity, while the threeand four-edit subsets (Sec. E.3) are deliberately smaller and built specifically to exercise multi-edit suppression, where two or more edits must be excluded at once. As result, the three-edit tier sends much larger share of its samples to the test split (160/268, 59.7%) than the two-edit tier does (55/1,535, 3.6%), with the four-edit tier close behind at 24/42 (57.1%). The large two-edit pool teaches the model the underlying structure of edit interactions rather than letting it memorize specific edit combinations. The threeand four-edit samples then extend this to cases where several unwanted edits must be suppressed together. Together, the two give balanced range of editing complexity, so the model generalizes across different numbers of edits while still suppressing edits reliably. Approach for training with dataset. We build training instances by pairing samples. For each setting in the training split, we form every possible pair of samples within that setting, assigning one sample to the analogy source (𝐴, 𝐴) and the other to the analogy target (𝐵, 𝐵), together with the edit descriptions for that setting. Each pair then yields several training instances, one for each retained subset available in that category (Sec. E.1). pair from 2-edit setting yields 3 instances (𝐼 {𝑒1 }, 𝐼 {𝑒2 }, 𝐼 ), while pair from 2-edit non-creature setting yields 2 (𝐼 {𝑒1 }, 𝐼 ). pair from 3-edit or 3-edit non-creature setting yields 3 (𝐼 {𝑒1 }, 𝐼 {𝑒1,𝑒2 }, 𝐼 ), and pair from 4-edit setting yields 4 (𝐼 {𝑒1 }, 𝐼 {𝑒1,𝑒2 }, 𝐼 {𝑒1,𝑒2,𝑒3 }, 𝐼 ). Applied across all training settings, this produces 23,992 effective training instances, which we find sufficient for our selective image analogy setting. Tab. 9 summarizes this calculation.

sections.title: G Evaluation Metric Details
sections.content: Selective image analogy places an unusual demand on evaluation: good output must apply the retained edits, avoid the suppressed edit, and otherwise leave the query image 𝐵 untouched. No single similarity score captures these three requirements at once. method that copies the full demonstration scores well on did the edits appear?, but fails on suppression. method that barely changes 𝐵 scores well on preservation but fails to apply anything. We therefore evaluate each output with structured, per-edit protocol rather than single holistic judgment. The main paper reports five metrics: three VLM-judge metrics (Retained Accuracy, Preservation, and Edit Recall) and two CLIP-based metrics (CLIP-Dir Image and CLIP-Dir Retained); we additionally report Suppression score in the ablation (Tab. 2). Below we give the full protocol behind these numbers: the structured VLM evaluation, the deterministic per-edit mapping, the consistency correction, and the SIA-aware extension of the LoRWeB [Manor et al. 2026] CLIP-directional metric. All metrics are computed for each (sample, method) pair and then aggregated in two stages: (i) the mean within each task triple (setting, data id, retained subset), and (ii) the mean across tasks. This two-step aggregation follows LoRWeB and prevents recipes with many retained-subset choices from dominating the final average. G.1 VLM single-image protocol Rather than asking the judge for single overall rating, which tends to be noisy and hard to reproduce, we ask it to reason about one edit at time and commit to discrete label, which we then map to number through fixed table. This keeps the judgment grounded in specific, checkable observations and removes most of the subjectivity from the numeric score. For each result, we show the judge the four images [𝐴, 𝐴, 𝐵, ˆ𝐵] with the retained and suppressed edit lists. The judge follows three-step evaluation protocol: STEP 1. Give brief factual description of ˆ𝐵. This anchors the later judgments in what is actually visible, rather than in what the edit lists say should be there. STEP 2. For each atomic edit 𝑒 E, describe the 𝐴 𝐴 change in the aspect named by 𝑒, describe the corresponding 𝐵 ˆ𝐵 change, and assign per-edit match label 𝑚(𝑒) {𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐}. The label records how closely the output reproduces the specific demonstrated change, not merely whether the right category of edit occurred: (𝑎) 𝐵 ˆ𝐵 reproduces 𝐴 𝐴 exactly, including the same specific instance. (𝑏) the same aspect changes, but with different specific instance. (𝑐) the aspect is unchanged. The judge also assigns an identity-match label 𝑚id {𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐} indicating whether ˆ𝐵 preserves the identity, layout, and unrelated content of 𝐵. STEP 3. Map each per-edit match label deterministically to binary detection flag 𝑑 (𝑒) {0, 1} and an integer score 𝑠 (𝑒) {1, . . . , 10} using Tab. 10. All judges use the identical prompt, metrics, and aggregation. They differ in absolute calibration, with Gemma 3 being more lenient overall, but all three rank SIA first on Retained Accuracy and Edit Recall. Tab. 11 reports the full comparison under all three judges. Consistency correction. The 110 score and the binary detection flag are both derived from the same match label. However, VLM responses occasionally break this coupling, for example by assigning high numeric score while also marking the edit as undetected. To keep Retained Accuracy consistent with the detection flags, we cap it at 2 when no retained edit is detected and at 5 when fewer than half of the retained edits are detected. No other corrections are applied to the metrics reported in the main paper. G.2 VLM metric definitions Let 𝑠 (𝑒) {1, . . . , 10} denote the consistency-corrected per-edit score, and let 𝑑 (𝑒) {0, 1} denote the detection flag. Recall that is the retained-edit set and = is the suppressed-edit set. SIA: Selective Image Analogy 19 Because the suppress role uses the inverted score ranges of Tab. 10, high Suppression score means the suppressed edits are correctly absent from ˆ𝐵. This metric targets the core requirement of selective transfer, which Preservation alone does not capture: method that leaves 𝐵 almost unchanged scores well on Preservation yet may still fail to remove suppressed edit that the demonstration would otherwise introduce. Suppression is defined only for partial-transfer samples, where . Preservation . Preservation is the 110 score obtained from the STEP-2 identity-match label, using the retain score ranges of Tab. 10: (𝑎) 910, (𝑏) 57, and (𝑐) 1. It reflects whether identity, layout, and unrelated content of 𝐵 are left intact. no-op method that returns ˆ𝐵 𝐵 will naturally score close to 10 on this metric, which is why Preservation must always be read together with Retained Accuracy and Suppression rather than on its own. Edit Recall . Edit Recall is the fraction of retained edits detected by the VLM: EditRecall = 1 𝑒 1[𝑑 (𝑒) = 1] . The indicator is 1 when edit 𝑒 is detected and 0 otherwise. Unlike Retained Accuracy, Recall only asks whether each wanted edit appeared at all, not whether it matches the demonstrated form. method can therefore reach high Recall while still scoring lower on Retained Accuracy. G.3 CLIP directional metrics The VLM metrics above are semantic and judge-dependent. We complement them with two lightweight, judge-independent CLIP directional metrics. The original CLIP-directional metric used by LoRWeB [Manor et al. 2026] assumes that ˆ𝐵 should reproduce the full transformation from 𝐴 to 𝐴. In selective image analogy, this assumption only holds for full-transfer samples. When the user suppresses an edit, ˆ𝐵 should intentionally disagree with the full 𝐴 𝐴 transformation along the suppressed-edit axis. As result, the original metric can incorrectly penalize correct selective output on partial-transfer samples. To address this, we also report textanchored directional metric built from the per-edit captions stored with each sample, following the text-driven CLIP-direction recipe popularized by StyleCLIP [Patashnik et al. 2021]. Suppression is the analogous average over the suppressed edits, and measures how well the output leaves out the edits the user chose to exclude: Supp = 1 𝑒 𝑠 (𝑒). Δ𝑇𝑅 = 𝜙𝑇 (𝑡𝑅) 𝜙𝑇 (𝑡src), where 𝑡src = photo, 𝑡𝑅 = photo with retained desc. is built from the per-edit captions of the retained set R. 20 Amirhossein Alimohammadi, Kian Izadpanah, Bardiya Kariminia, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, and Ali Mahdavi-Amiri Table 11. This is the original LoRWeB image-image directional metric, which checks whether the output moves through image space in the same direction as the demonstrated edit: CLIPDirImage = cos (cid:0)Δ𝐼𝐴, Δ𝐼 (cid:1). We compute it only on full-transfer samples (R = E). It is reported as NaN on partial-transfer rows because Δ𝐼𝐴 also includes the suppressed edits in those cases and would penalize correct selective output. CLIP-Dir Retained . This is our SIA-aware text-anchored directional metric: CLIPDirRetained = cos (cid:0)Δ𝐼, Δ𝑇𝑅 (cid:1). It replaces the demonstrated image-space direction with the direction described by the retained-edit text, so it is defined for every sample, including partial transfers, and measures whether ˆ𝐵 moves toward the retained-edit description regardless of what the suppressed edits do. It therefore serves as the selective-transfer counterpart of CLIPDirImage when no full-transfer ground truth is available. Both CLIP metrics are judge-independent and are computed once for the full benchmark. G.4 VLM Evaluation Prompt For reproducibility, we include the evaluation prompt. It restates the three-step protocol of Sec. G.1. The box fixes the exact output schema, which we parse to obtain the per-edit fields used by the metrics in Sec. G.2. The VLM receives the four images [𝐴, 𝐴, 𝐵, ˆ𝐵] together with the retainedand suppressed-edit lists. VLM Evaluation Prompt You are evaluating selective image analogy result. You are given: (1) Image 𝐴: the original demonstration image. (2) Image 𝐴: the edited version of Image 𝐴. (3) Image 𝐵: the query image to edit. (4) Output ˆ𝐵: the generated result. (5) Retained edits: edits that should appear in the output. (6) Suppressed edits: edits that should not appear in the output. STEP 1. Describe the output ˆ𝐵 briefly. STEP 2. The cases in Figs. 14 17 were selected from the 60 benchmark cases rendered with that prompt order. We kept cases without visible leak of an excluded edit, without mismatch between retained edit and the one in 𝐴, and without artifacts. They show what the model does well and are not random sample. We also saw failures that the judge does not penalize strongly. The attribute that is added to query image tends to take generic form for that person, so an accessory matches the one in 𝐴 closely only when 𝐴 already resembles that generic form. style edit can tint hair or clothes, background edit is subtle when 𝐵 already shows similar scene, and style or pencil edit is sometimes only half applied when the background edit is dropped. The four-edit case of Fig. 15 has weak tiles as well: with the crown, the green hair and the Paris background retained, and no style, the subject is reframed and smaller than in 𝐵, and in several tiles the crown hides most of the green hair. Because the benchmark covers proper subsets only, the all-edits outputs in Figs. 1517 were generated separately with the same weights (AnaLoRA at 2K and ExLoRA at 5K steps), without suppression, with seed 0, 40 steps and 512 px. SIA on Qwen-Image-2.1 All experiments in the main paper, including the quantitative tables, the comparisons with baselines, the ablations and the user studies, use Flux.2-Klein. In addition, we trained SIA on second, more recent backbone, Qwen-Image-2.1, from the Qwen-Image family [Wu et al. 2025]. This suggests that the method is not tied to one backbone: the same two stages and the same training data carry over. In our informal inspection the Qwen-Image-2.1 outputs also look visually better than the Flux.2-Klein ones, possibly because the backbone is more recent; we did not measure this. The QwenImage-2.1 model uses AnaLoRA and ExLoRA without CSV, and we did not repeat the baseline comparisons, the ablations or the user studies for it, so every claim in the main paper refers to Flux.2-Klein only. Figs. 1417 show curated results of this model. Training. We follow the two-stage recipe of Sec. and train on the same training split of our multi-edit analogy dataset (Sec. E). Both stages use Qwen-Image-2.1 at 512 px, LoRA rank 𝑟 =16, batch size 16 and seed 0. The learning rates were chosen with short sweep of AnaLoRA runs, so they, and the ExLoRA batch size, differ from the Flux.2-Klein values. AnaLoRA is trained with learning rate 2104, with the prompt dropped for 15% of the samples, and we use the checkpoint after 2K steps. ExLoRA is initialized from that checkpoint and trained with learning rate 2104, while the jointly updated AnaLoRA weights use 5105 and an anchoring weight of 0.1, as for Flux.2-Klein. ExLoRA is trained for about 6.5K steps and we use the checkpoint after 5K steps. This checkpoint was selected on half of the test set, where the checkpoints between 3K and 6K steps are close (average 9.559.62), so the scores below are slightly optimistic. To apply the suppression mask to the prompt tokens of the excluded edits, we map the tokens of each edit phrase to the rows of the prompt embedding and to the joint textimage token sequence consumed by the transformer. At inference we use 40 denoising steps without classifier-free guidance. Prompt order at inference. For the figures in this section, the retained edits are listed first in the prompt and the excluded edits last. This is change of the prompt only and needs no retraining. On quarter of the benchmark (352 items from 60 cases) it raises the judge average by 0.20 over the default order (the output is better for 34 items, worse for 11 and unchanged for 307; sign test 𝑝=0.0008). All of the gain is on edit subsets that the training data does not cover. Evaluation. We evaluate on the 239 test cases, scoring every nonempty proper subset of the edits (1,406 items) with Qwen3-VL-32BInstruct, using one image and one seed per item. The judge scores Retained Accuracy, Suppression and Preservation on 010 scale. Unlike Sec. G, this protocol has no consistency correction and uses plain mean, so the numbers are not comparable with the main tables. Tab. 12 compares ExLoRA with deleting the excluded edits from the AnaLoRA prompt: prompt deletion lowers Suppression from 9.94 to 7.26. The judge is lenient, however: returning 𝐵 unchanged scores 10.00 on Suppression and Preservation but only 1.09 on Retained Accuracy, so high Suppression score alone is not evidence of quality. Adding CSV on top of the trained ExLoRA gave no measurable gain, so we use ExLoRA without CSV on Qwen-Image-2.1. SIA: Selective Image Analogy 25 Fig. 13.
